structure.overview: Mr. Isaac Smeele sought judicial review of a CRA Officer's decision denying his eligibility for the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB) on the basis that his Airbnb and car rental income was rental income, not self-employment income, and thus did not meet the income threshold. The CRA Officer and subsequent reviewers consistently found Mr. Smeele ineligible, and the court found no reviewable error in the Officer's decision, dismissing the application. The court emphasized that new evidence and arguments not before the Officer could not be considered and that the burden of proof lay with Mr. Smeele.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant Mr. Isaac Smeele seeks judicial review of CRA Officer's decision denying his eligibility for the Canada recovery benefit due to not meeting income threshold.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court expresses sympathy for Mr. Smeele but finds no reviewable error in Officer's decision and dismisses the judicial review application.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court outlines background: CRB introduced Sept 2020; Mr. Smeele applied Oct 12, 2020, received payments, and his file was selected for eligibility review in Jan 2021.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele provided documents showing Airbnb and car rental income in 2019 but initially reported a net loss on his tax return; he later applied to amend his 2019 return.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: First Reviewer denied Mr. Smeele's CRB application on Aug 5, 2021, finding he did not meet income threshold or income reduction requirement under the Act.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Second Reviewer informed Mr. Smeele in Oct 2021 that Airbnb and car rental income were rental income, not self-employment income, thus ineligible for CRB; denied application Nov 3, 2021.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele sought judicial review but discontinued it when CRA agreed to a third review to consider new information including a CRA interpretation bulletin on rental property.
idea_list: New info submitted including interpretation bulletin

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele submitted affidavits describing extra services provided to Airbnb guests, arguing this made the income self-employment income, not rental income.
idea_list: Affidavits from Mr. Smeele and family

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer refused Mr. Smeele's CRB application on Mar 18, 2022, again finding income was rental income and did not meet minimum income threshold.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found host and cleaning fees combined were below $5,000 threshold and no other income breakdown was provided, concluding Mr. Smeele did not qualify for CRB.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Attorney General requested and court agreed to amend style of cause to name Attorney General as proper respondent.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Issue is whether Officer reasonably determined Mr. Smeele was ineligible for CRB due to income threshold; standard of review is reasonableness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court notes Mr. Smeele's judicial review relies on facts and arguments not before Officer, who considered whether Airbnb income was self-employment or rental income.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele argued before CRA that Airbnb income was self-employment income based on interpretation bulletin and provided evidence of fees and services.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer determined Airbnb income was rental income and extra services did not change that, considering the interpretation bulletin.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Before court, Mr. Smeele raised a new argument about a $6,000 art sale in 2019 not included in income, supported by affidavit but no bank proof.
idea_list: New argument about art sale income

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court explains it must decide reasonableness based on information before Officer at decision time, so new arguments not considered by Officer are difficult to accept.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds Officer reasonably concluded extra services did not convert Airbnb income to self-employment income, citing case law.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Monetary breakdown of extra services was less than $5,000, insufficient to meet minimum income threshold even if considered self-employment income.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele's partner argued the Airbnb was a true business space for artists, not just a side investment, but this was not supported by affidavit.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court notes bigger business picture was not before Officer, who only had minimal evidence of extra services and found income was rental income.
idea_list: No broader business model evidence before Officer
Income found to be rental income

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court states if Mr. Smeele had submitted fuller business model evidence, Officer's decision might differ, but burden is on claimant and Officer not obliged to make claimant's case.
idea_list: Burden on claimant to prove case

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application and orders no costs.
